lesson_scope: Equilibrium of particles on rough inclined planes; Coulomb static and kinetic friction laws on inclines; single limiting equilibrium thresholds (slipping up versus slipping down); natural angle of repose; holding forces applied parallel, horizontally, and at optimal angles; connected particles over crest pulleys; and two connected blocks with differential friction coefficients.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Normal reaction and maximum static friction on a rough incline

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Normal reaction and maximum static friction on a rough incline

hints: Resolve forces perpendicular to the incline to find the normal reaction: $R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 40\cos 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6\text{ N}$.
Use Coulomb's limiting friction law: $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.4(20\sqrt{3}) = 8\sqrt{3} \approx 13.9\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_\perp = R - mg\cos 30^\circ = 0$$
$$R = 4(10)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6410 \approx 34.6\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum static friction force available from the surface:
$$F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.4(20\sqrt{3}) = 8\sqrt{3} \approx 13.8564 \approx 13.9\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find the contact reaction into the slope:
- Normal reaction supports the perpendicular weight:
$$R = 40\cos 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6\text{ N}$$

Calculate friction grip limit:
- Multiply by the coefficient of friction $\mu = 0.4$:
$$F_{\max} = 0.4 \times 20\sqrt{3} = 8\sqrt{3} \approx 13.9\text{ N}$$
The surface can provide at most $13.9\text{ N}$ of grip.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to plane: $R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6\text{ N}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 2: Angle of repose and natural sliding threshold under gravity

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 2: Angle of repose and natural sliding threshold under gravity

hints: When the crate is on the point of slipping down under gravity alone, downhill weight equals limiting friction: $mg\sin\theta_c = \mu R$.
Substitute $R = mg\cos\theta_c$ to get $mg\sin\theta_c = \mu mg\cos\theta_c \implies \tan\theta_c = \mu = 0.75$, so $\theta_c = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.9^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Set up limiting equilibrium along the incline with friction acting up the slope:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = mg\sin\theta_c - F_{\max} = 0$$
$$mg\sin\theta_c = \mu mg\cos\theta_c$$

Divide by $mg\cos\theta_c$ to obtain the angle of friction relationship:
$$\tan\theta_c = \mu = 0.75$$
$$\theta_c = \tan^{-1}(0.75) \approx 36.8699^\circ \approx 36.9^\circ$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Equate downhill slip to friction grip:
- At the sliding threshold, gravity matches limiting friction:
$$mg\sin\theta_c = \mu mg\cos\theta_c$$

Notice mass cancels out completely:
$$\tan\theta_c = \mu = 0.75 \implies \theta_c \approx 36.9^\circ$$
The crate begins sliding as soon as the slope reaches $36.9^\circ$, regardless of its mass.

ai_rubric.observable: Equates downhill weight component to limiting friction: $mg\sin\theta_c = \mu mg\cos\theta_c \implies \tan\theta_c = \mu$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 3: Minimum holding force parallel to slope to prevent downward slip

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 3: Minimum holding force parallel to slope to prevent downward slip

hints: When the particle is on the point of slipping down, friction acts up the slope to oppose motion.

Form the force balance along the slope: $P + F_{\max} = mg\sin 30^\circ$, where $F_{\max} = \mu mg\cos 30^\circ = 0.2(25\sqrt{3}) = 5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.66\text{ N}$. Thus $P = 25 - 8.66 = 16.3\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane to find normal reaction:
$$R = mg\cos 30^\circ = 5(10)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 25\sqrt{3} \approx 43.3013\text{ N}$$

Resolve forces along the slope in limiting equilibrium (friction acting up):
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = P + \mu R - mg\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$P = 50(0.5) - 0.2(25\sqrt{3}) = 25 - 5\sqrt{3} \approx 25 - 8.6603 = 16.3397 \approx 16.3\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Identify the motion tendency:
- The block wants to slip down, so friction helps the holding force by pointing uphill:
$$P + F_{\max} = mg\sin 30^\circ$$

Compute the minimum pull:
- Downhill gravity is $25\text{ N}$ and friction assists with $5\sqrt{3} \approx 8.66\text{ N}$:
$$P = 25 - 8.66 = 16.3\text{ N}$$
A pull of $16.3\text{ N}$ up the slope prevents sliding.

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves along slope with friction acting up: $P + \mu(50\cos 30^\circ) = 50\sin 30^\circ$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 4: Pulling up a rough incline at constant speed

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 4: Pulling up a rough incline at constant speed

hints: At constant speed, acceleration is zero ($a = 0$), so the forces parallel to the plane balance.
Because the sled moves up the slope, friction acts down the slope: $T = mg\sin 15^\circ + \mu mg\cos 15^\circ = 200\sin 15^\circ + 0.15(200\cos 15^\circ) \approx 80.7\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve perpendicular to the incline to find the normal reaction $R$:
$$R = mg\cos 15^\circ = 200\cos 15^\circ \approx 193.1852\text{ N}$$
$$F = \mu R = 0.15(193.1852) \approx 28.9778\text{ N}$$

Resolve parallel to the incline with zero acceleration ($a = 0$):
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = T - mg\sin 15^\circ - F = 0$$
$$T = 200\sin 15^\circ + 28.9778 \approx 51.7638 + 28.9778 = 80.7416 \approx 80.7\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find the resisting forces opposing upward motion:
- Downhill gravity component: $200\sin 15^\circ \approx 51.76\text{ N}$.
- Downhill dynamic friction:
$$F_f = 0.15(200\cos 15^\circ) \approx 28.98\text{ N}$$

Sum the opposing forces:
- At steady speed, tension overcomes both gravity and friction:
$$T = 51.76 + 28.98 = 80.7\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Calculates friction opposing upward motion: $F = \mu(200\cos 15^\circ) = 0.15(193.19) \approx 28.98\text{ N}$.
Forms equilibrium along slope at constant speed: $T = 200\sin 15^\circ + 28.98 \approx 51.76 + 28.98 = 80.7\text{ N}$.

Since downhill gravity $mg\sin 20^\circ = 60\sin 20^\circ \approx 20.5212\text{ N} < F_{\max}$, the block is stationary.

Determine the actual frictional force from equilibrium along the slope:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = mg\sin 20^\circ - F_f = 0$$
$$F_f = 60\sin 20^\circ \approx 20.5212 \approx 20.5\text{ N} \quad (\text{acting up the slope})$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:

- Maximum available grip is $33.8\text{ N}$.
- Downhill gravity is only $20.5\text{ N}$:
$$W_\parallel = 60\sin 20^\circ \approx 20.5\text{ N} < F_{\max}$$

State the actual friction:
- Static friction only provides what is needed to maintain rest:
$$F_f = 20.5\text{ N} \quad (\text{up the slope})$$
It does not reach the $33.8\text{ N}$ limit.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 6: Horizontal pushing force to prevent downward slipping

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 6: Horizontal pushing force to prevent downward slipping

hints: Tendency of motion is down the slope, so friction acts up the slope: $F = \mu R = 0.5 R$.

Express $R$ perpendicular to slope: $R = 20\cos 45^\circ + P\sin 45^\circ = \frac{20 + P}{\sqrt{2}}$. Substitute into parallel equilibrium: $P\cos 45^\circ + 0.5 R = 20\sin 45^\circ \implies P + 0.5(20 + P) = 20 \implies 1.5P = 10 \implies P = \frac{20}{3} \approx 6.67\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the plane to express the normal reaction $R$:
$$R = mg\cos 45^\circ + P\sin 45^\circ = 20\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) + P\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{20 + P}{\sqrt{2}}$$

Resolve forces along the line of greatest slope with limiting friction acting up:
$$P\cos 45^\circ + \mu R - mg\sin 45^\circ = 0$$
$$\frac{P}{\sqrt{2}} + 0.5\left(\frac{20 + P}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = \frac{20}{\sqrt{2}}$$
$$P + 10 + 0.5P = 20 \implies 1.5P = 10 \implies P = \frac{20}{3} \approx 6.6667 \approx 6.67\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Set up force equations for downward slip limit:
- Reaction includes horizontal push contribution:
$$R = \frac{20 + P}{\sqrt{2}}$$
- Uphill push and friction balance downhill gravity:
$$P\cos 45^\circ + 0.5 R = 20\sin 45^\circ$$

Cancel the common factor of $1/\sqrt{2}$ and solve:
$$1.5P = 10 \implies P = \frac{20}{3} \approx 6.67\text{ N}$$
A horizontal push of $6.67\text{ N}$ suffices to prevent sliding.

ai_rubric.observable: Forms equilibrium along slope with friction up: $P\cos 45^\circ + 0.5(20\cos 45^\circ + P\sin 45^\circ) = 20\sin 45^\circ$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Core Practice 1: Crate pulled up rough slope with exact Pythagorean gradient ratios

hints: The downhill component of gravity is $mg\sin\alpha = 260\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 100\text{ N}$.
When moving up at constant speed, friction acts down, so $P_1 = 100 + 60 = 160\text{ N}$. When held from slipping down, friction acts up, so $P_0 + 60 = 100 \implies P_0 = 40\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate the downhill component of gravity:
$$W_\parallel = mg\sin\alpha = 260\left(\frac{5}{13}\right) = 100\text{ N}$$

Calculate the force $P_1$ to move up the plane at constant speed (friction opposing upward motion acts down):
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = P_1 - W_\parallel - F_{\max} = 0$$
$$P_1 = 100 + 60 = 160\text{ N}$$

Calculate the minimum force $P_0$ to prevent downward sliding (friction opposing downward motion acts up):
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = P_0 + F_{\max} - W_\parallel = 0$$
$$P_0 = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find downhill gravity component:
$$W_\parallel = 260 \times \frac{5}{13} = 100\text{ N}$$

Compute upward pulling force:
- Pulling up overcomes both gravity and friction:
$$P_1 = 100 + 60 = 160\text{ N}$$

Compute downward holding threshold:
- Uphill friction assists, so holding force only needs to cover the remainder:
$$P_0 = 100 - 60 = 40\text{ N}$$
Any force between $40\text{ N}$ and $160\text{ N}$ keeps the crate at rest.

$$R = 80 + 0.6P$$

Reverse friction for upward slip:
- Uphill push $0.8P$ must overcome both gravity ($60\text{ N}$) and downhill friction ($40 + 0.3P$):
$$0.8P = 60 + (40 + 0.3P)$$

Collect terms:
$$0.5P = 100\text{ N}$$

Evaluate maximum holding push:
$$P_{\max} = 200\text{ N}$$
The block remains at rest for any push $P$ in the range $\frac{200}{11}\text{ N} \leqslant P \leqslant 200\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 1: Optimal pulling angle on a rough inclined plane

hints: Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane: the tension has an upward lifting component $T\sin\theta$, so $R = 500\cos 30^\circ - T\sin\theta$.
Resolve forces parallel to the inclined plane: because the case is on the verge of slipping up, friction acts down the slope: $T\cos\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + \mu R$.
Substitute the expression for $R$ into the parallel equation: $T\cos\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + \mu(500\cos 30^\circ - T\sin\theta)$.
Collect all terms containing $T$ on the left-hand side: $T\cos\theta + \mu T\sin\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + 500\mu\cos 30^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Resolve forces perpendicular to the inclined plane in equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_\perp = R + T\sin\theta - W\cos 30^\circ = 0$$
$$R = 500\cos 30^\circ - T\sin\theta$$

Resolve forces along the line of greatest slope with limiting friction opposing upward motion:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = T\cos\theta - W\sin 30^\circ - \mu R = 0$$
$$T\cos\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + \mu(500\cos 30^\circ - T\sin\theta)$$

Expand and collect the tension terms on the left side:
$$T\cos\theta + \mu T\sin\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + 500\mu\cos 30^\circ$$
$$T(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta) = 500(\sin 30^\circ + \mu\cos 30^\circ)$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find normal reaction with angled pull:
- The rope lifts part of the weight off the slope:
$$R = 500\cos 30^\circ - T\sin\theta$$

Balance forces along the slope:
- Forward pull $T\cos\theta$ counters downhill gravity and friction:
$$T\cos\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + \mu R$$

Substitute $R$ and group terms:
- Moving $T\sin\theta$ to the left yields:
$$T(\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta) = 500(\sin 30^\circ + \mu\cos 30^\circ)$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves along slope with friction down: $T\cos\theta = 500\sin 30^\circ + \mu R$.

hints: Substitute $\mu = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ into the right-hand side: $500\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 500(0.5 + 0.5) = 500\text{ N}$.

Express the denominator $\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta$ in harmonic form: $\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\right) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$.
To minimize $T = \frac{500}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)}$, maximize the cosine term at $\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 1 \implies \theta = 30^\circ$.
Compute $T_{\min} = 250\sqrt{3} \approx 433\text{ N}$ and substitute back to find normal reaction: $R = 500\cos 30^\circ - T_{\min}\sin 30^\circ = 125\sqrt{3} \approx 217\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Evaluate the constant right-hand side using $\mu = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$:
$$500(\sin 30^\circ + \mu\cos 30^\circ) = 500\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 500(0.5 + 0.5) = 500\text{ N}$$

Rewrite the angular factor in the left-hand side using the angle addition identity:
$$\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\cos\theta + \frac{1}{2}\sin\theta\right) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$$

Minimize tension with respect to angle $\theta$:
$$T = \frac{500}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)}$$
The tension is minimized when the denominator is maximized:
$$\cos(\theta - 30^\circ) = 1 \implies \theta = 30^\circ$$
$$T_{\min} = \frac{500}{\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}} = 250\sqrt{3} \approx 433.0127 \approx 433\text{ N}$$

Calculate the corresponding normal reaction $R$ at this optimal angle:
$$R = 500\cos 30^\circ - T_{\min}\sin 30^\circ = 500\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) - (250\sqrt{3})(0.5) = 250\sqrt{3} - 125\sqrt{3} = 125\sqrt{3} \approx 216.5064 \approx 217\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Simplify the equation:
- Substituting $\mu = 1/\sqrt{3}$ makes the right side exactly $500\text{ N}$:
$$T\left(\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta\right) = 500\text{ N}$$

Apply the harmonic identity:
- The bracket reaches its peak when pulling at the angle of friction $\theta = \lambda = 30^\circ$:
$$\cos\theta + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\sin\theta = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\cos(\theta - 30^\circ)$$

Find the minimum tension:
- At $\theta = 30^\circ$, the pulling efficiency is maximized:
$$T_{\min} = 250\sqrt{3} \approx 433\text{ N}$$

Calculate the reaction force:
$$R = 125\sqrt{3} \approx 217\text{ N}$$
Pulling at $30^\circ$ above the slope reduces the required pull to $433\text{ N}$.

hints: Calculate normal reactions for each block independently: $R_P = m_P g\cos 30^\circ = 40\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$ and $R_Q = m_Q g\cos 30^\circ = 60\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 30\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$.
Multiply each reaction by its respective coefficient of friction: $F_{P,\max} = \mu_P R_P$ and $F_{Q,\max} = \mu_Q R_Q$.
For block $P$: $F_{P,\max} = 0.2(20\sqrt{3}) = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93\text{ N}$.
For block $Q$: $F_{Q,\max} = 0.5(30\sqrt{3}) = 15\sqrt{3} \approx 25.98 \approx 26.0\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Calculate normal reactions perpendicular to the slope for each block:
$$R_P = m_P g\cos 30^\circ = 4(10)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.6410\text{ N}$$
$$R_Q = m_Q g\cos 30^\circ = 6(10)\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 30\sqrt{3} \approx 51.9615\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum available static friction for block $P$:
$$F_{P,\max} = \mu_P R_P = 0.2(20\sqrt{3}) = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.9282 \approx 6.93\text{ N}$$

Calculate the maximum available static friction for block $Q$:
$$F_{Q,\max} = \mu_Q R_Q = 0.5(30\sqrt{3}) = 15\sqrt{3} \approx 25.9808 \approx 26.0\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find normal forces on each mass:
- Block $P$: $R_P = 20\sqrt{3} \approx 34.64\text{ N}$.
- Block $Q$:
$$R_Q = 30\sqrt{3} \approx 51.96\text{ N}$$

Compute individual friction limits:
- Block $P$ has a smoother surface ($\mu = 0.2$):
$$F_{P,\max} = 0.2 \times 20\sqrt{3} = 4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93\text{ N}$$

Evaluate block $Q$ friction limit:
- Block $Q$ has a rougher surface ($\mu = 0.5$):
$$F_{Q,\max} = 0.5 \times 30\sqrt{3} = 15\sqrt{3} \approx 26.0\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Resolves perpendicular to plane for both blocks: $R_P = 40\cos 30^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$ and $R_Q = 60\cos 30^\circ = 30\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$.

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Capstone Practice 2: Connected blocks with differential friction on rough slope

hints: Sum the downhill gravity components for the combined system: $(4 + 6)(10)\sin 30^\circ = 50\text{ N}$.
Compare this with the total available uphill friction from both blocks: $F_{\text{total}} = 4\sqrt{3} + 15\sqrt{3} = 19\sqrt{3} \approx 32.91\text{ N}$.
Because $50\text{ N} > 32.91\text{ N}$, gravity overpowers friction, so the two blocks must slide down if unsupported.

Block $P$ is higher up and has smaller friction coefficient ($\mu_P = 0.2$ vs $\mu_Q = 0.5$). If unlinked, $P$ would slide faster than $Q$. Therefore, $P$ shoves against $Q$, putting the rod under compression (thrust).

walkthrough.text:
Compare total downhill force against total maximum friction for the two-block system:
$$\text{Total downhill weight} = (m_P + m_Q)g\sin 30^\circ = (4 + 6)(10)(0.5) = 50\text{ N}$$
$$\text{Total maximum friction} = F_{P,\max} + F_{Q,\max} = 4\sqrt{3} + 15\sqrt{3} = 19\sqrt{3} \approx 32.9090\text{ N}$$

Assess equilibrium viability:
Because the downhill gravitational force ($50\text{ N}$) exceeds the total maximum possible friction ($32.91\text{ N}$), static equilibrium under gravity alone is impossible without an external holding force:
$$50\text{ N} > 19\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$$

Determine the state of the rod:
Compare individual sliding tendencies:
- Block $P$: net downhill tendency per unit mass is $g\sin 30^\circ - \mu_P g\cos 30^\circ = 5 - 0.2(10)(0.866) \approx 3.27\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
- Block $Q$: net downhill tendency per unit mass is $g\sin 30^\circ - \mu_Q g\cos 30^\circ = 5 - 0.5(10)(0.866) \approx 0.67\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Because block $P$ is positioned higher up the slope and experiences less friction than block $Q$, it bears down upon $Q$. Hence, the rod is subjected to thrust:
$$\text{Rod state} = \text{compression (thrust)}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Check if gravity or friction wins:
- Combined downhill pull: $10 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 50\text{ N}$.
- Total friction available:
$$F_\text{total} = 19\sqrt{3} \approx 32.9\text{ N}$$

Conclude on equilibrium:
- Gravity ($50\text{ N}$) exceeds friction ($32.9\text{ N}$), so both blocks will accelerate downhill unless an external force intervenes:
$$W_\parallel > F_\text{total}$$

Determine rod stress:
- Block $P$ is more slippery than block $Q$ ($\mu_P = 0.2 < 0.5$), so it wants to slide faster.
- Being above $Q$, it pushes directly into $Q$:
$$\text{Rod is in compression}$$

Concludes that equilibrium is impossible because downhill gravity exceeds total friction: $50\text{ N} > 32.91\text{ N}$.

Explains that because the higher block $P$ is on a more slippery surface ($\mu_P = 0.2 < \mu_Q = 0.5$), it tries to accelerate faster than $Q$, pushing against $Q$ so the rod is in compression (thrust).

hints: Consider the combined system along the incline: the holding force and both friction forces act uphill to balance total downhill gravity: $F_{\text{hold}} + 19\sqrt{3} = 50$.
Solve for the holding force: $F_{\text{hold}} = 50 - 19\sqrt{3} \approx 50 - 32.91 = 17.09 \approx 17.1\text{ N}$.

To find the thrust $C$ in the rod, isolate block $P$: the forces along the slope are downhill gravity ($40\sin 30^\circ = 20\text{ N}$), uphill friction ($4\sqrt{3} \approx 6.93\text{ N}$), and uphill thrust from the rod $C$.
Form equilibrium for block $P$: $C + 4\sqrt{3} = 20 \implies C = 20 - 4\sqrt{3} \approx 13.07 \approx 13.1\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Apply equilibrium along the line of greatest slope for the combined two-block system:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = F_{\text{hold}} + F_{P,\max} + F_{Q,\max} - (m_P + m_Q)g\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$F_{\text{hold}} + 4\sqrt{3} + 15\sqrt{3} = 50$$

Calculate the minimum holding force $F_{\text{hold}}$:
$$F_{\text{hold}} = 50 - 19\sqrt{3} \approx 50 - 32.9090 = 17.0910 \approx 17.1\text{ N}$$

Isolate block $P$ to determine the thrust (compressive force) $C$ transmitted through the rod:
$$\Sigma F_\parallel = C + F_{P,\max} - m_P g\sin 30^\circ = 0$$
$$C + 4\sqrt{3} - 40(0.5) = 0$$
$$C = 20 - 4\sqrt{3} \approx 20 - 6.9282 = 13.0718 \approx 13.1\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the entire system:
- Gravity pulls down with $50\text{ N}$.
- Both blocks provide total friction of $19\sqrt{3} \approx 32.91\text{ N}$:
$$F_{\text{hold}} + 32.91 = 50\text{ N}$$

Find holding force on block $Q$:
$$F_{\text{hold}} = 50 - 32.91 = 17.1\text{ N}$$

Isolate block $P$ to find internal thrust:
- Block $P$ needs $20\text{ N}$ to balance gravity, and its own friction provides $6.93\text{ N}$.
- The rod must push back with the difference:
$$C = 20 - 6.93 = 13.1\text{ N}$$
The rod transmits a compressive thrust of $13.1\text{ N}$.
